snippet.title: 1100s AD: What People Used to Eat at Medieval Alehouses (England)
snippet.description:
Forget the roaring fireplaces, perfectly roasted meats, and merry singing dwarves you see in Hollywood fantasy movies. If you stepped foot into an actual English tavern in the 1100s, the smell alone would knock you flat. Discover the grueling, filthy, and fascinating reality of what people really ate, drank, and endured to survive the Middle Ages.

In this video, we cover:

Inside the "Alehouse": Why the local tavern wasn't a pub, but a cramped, smoke-filled, wattle-and-daub hut shared with farm animals.

Liquid Bread: The shocking reason why absolutely everyone—including young children—drank thick, cloudy, and bitter ale from sunrise to sunset.

The Ultimate Survival Diet: The truth about "pottage" (the endless, simmering vegetable stew) and the rock-hard bread peasants used as edible plates.

After Dark: The high-stakes dice games, violent brawls, and the strict curfews that dictated the only free time these exhausted workers ever had.

If you enjoyed this deep dive into the 12th century, hit that Like button, Subscribe for more unvarnished history, and let me know in the comments: what historical era or event should we uncover next?

In this video, we explore 10 practical medieval methods used to survive extreme cold without modern heating systems.

You’ll Discover:
How people trapped heat inside stone and wooden homes
The role of layers, wool, and natural fabrics in staying warm
Why sleeping arrangements made a huge difference
Simple ways fires were used more efficiently
How daily routines helped conserve body heat

No heaters. No electricity. Just clever solutions developed through necessity.

Sometimes the best way to stay warm… is the way people did it centuries ago.

snippet.title: The Royal Secrets of Edinburgh Castle | Luxury, Power and Cliff Escapes (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
"Edinburgh Castle stands on a volcanic rock high above Scotland’s capital, but behind the postcards lies a far darker story. Once a lavish royal palace where Mary Queen of Scots gave birth to a future king, it became a ruthless military stronghold torn apart by the Lang Siege, then one of Britain’s grimmest prisons of war. Walk the damp vaults where French, American and other POWs carved their names and plotted daring escapes down the sheer rock face. Feel the weight of centuries of power, betrayal, survival — and even a quiet dog cemetery that tells its own tale of loyalty. This is the real, unflinching history of Edinburgh Castle."

Lessons learned from this video:

Power and luxury are fragile — the same walls that hosted royal banquets later became dungeons for the defeated.
Human resilience thrives even in the darkest places, from desperate escapes to tiny carvings left by prisoners.
War turns palaces into prisons and ordinary lives into stories of endurance and loss.
History is layered in stone — what we see today hides centuries of both grandeur and suffering.
Small acts of humanity can outlast the violence that defines a place.

Reliable Sources:
Official Edinburgh Castle website – full history overview, royal residence until 1633, shift to military stronghold and prison: https://www.edinburghcastle.scot/the-castle/history/
Edinburgh Castle official blog – detailed article on Prisons of War (1757–1814), French privateers in 1758, conditions in the vaults: https://blog.edinburghcastle.scot/edinburgh-castle-prisons-war/
Edinburgh Castle official blog – 1811 mass escape of 49 French POWs through the Devil’s Elbow using washing lines: https://blog.edinburghcastle.scot/ten-epic-attempts-to-escape-edinburgh-castle/

snippet.title: The Medieval Secret to Keeping Pests Out of Your Garden Forever
snippet.description:
Long before chemical pesticides existed, medieval gardeners had to protect their crops using simple, natural methods. Surprisingly, many of these techniques were incredibly effective and some are still used by organic gardeners today.

In this video, we uncover the old gardening strategies medieval growers used to keep pests away while protecting their soil and crops.

You’ll Discover:

Companion planting combinations that naturally repel insects

Herbs and plants medieval gardeners used as pest deterrents

Natural barriers that kept pests away from crops

Soil and crop rotation tricks that reduced infestations

Why traditional gardens often had fewer pest problems

No chemicals. No modern pesticides. Just smart planting methods developed through centuries of practical farming.

Sometimes the best garden defense… is the oldest one.

Vengeance is a mix of anger, hatred, and righteous fury, the emotional fuel that makes someone feel not only wronged but absolutely justified in settling the score. snippet.title: The incredible engineering of Venice - Stephanie H. Smith
snippet.description:
Explore the history of Venice to find out how the infamous floating city was built and how the republic became a hub for trade.

--

To escape Germanic invaders, people fled into the Venetian Lagoon in the 6th century. The settlers set out to tame the mudflats and built a foundation in the marshy maze to support heavier, longer-lasting structures. Little did they know, this system of wood, water, and mud would still be supporting an infamous floating city 1,500 years later. Stephanie H. Smith explores the history of Venice.

snippet.title: The Alaska Purchase – debunking a myth
snippet.description:
There is a common historical myth among Americans that the Alaska Purchase in 1867 was deeply unpopular -- that Americans didn't see any value in it and ridiculed it as "Seward's Folly" and "Seward's Icebox". But in reality there was widespread support for the purchase. Most of the newspaper reporting at the time was positive or at least neutral, and the treaty easily passed the Senate.

There were three main reasons for American support for the Alaska Purchase:
1. Americans and Russians did in fact know (contrary to the modern myth) that Alaska was rich in natural resources.
2. Many Americans believed that control of Alaska would make it easier to trade with Asia. (Americans had been trading with Asia since colonial times.)
3. Most Americans were in favor of annexing the British colonies north of the U.S. (what later became Canada), and they saw the acquisition of Alaska as furthering that goal.

One point I didn't make in the video but is worth noting:
The Senate passed the Alaska Purchase treaty 37-2. Some modern sources erroneously claim that the purchase "barely passed by one vote". Not true. The Constitution says the Senate ratifies a treaty with two-thirds of those voting, not two-thirds of all members. So the treaty got 95% of the Senate vote, well above the 67% necessary. The Alaska Purchase had bipartisan support during one of the most politically divided periods in American history.

snippet.title: The Famine That Broke Europe Before the Black Death (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
This video covers the full story — what life looked like before the famine, what caused it, how people and the English crown scrambled to survive, and what the world looked like after. It also explains why this largely forgotten disaster directly set the stage for the Black Death decades later.

Lessons Learned From This Video:
1) A civilization built with zero surplus margin is one bad season away from total collapse.
2) Price controls don't work when there's nothing to sell at any price.
3) The people at the top of a broken system still fall — Edward II couldn't find bread at a royal abbey.
4) The things that feel permanent — good weather, full fields, stable society — are always more fragile than they look.
5) History's most transformative shifts in power often start not with revolution, but with a famine that proves the old order is hollow.

Sources:
1. Academic Books:William Chester Jordan — The Great Famine: Northern Europe in the Early Fourteenth Century, Princeton University Press, 1996
2. Bruce M.S. Campbell — The Great Transition: Climate, Disease and Society in the Late Medieval World, Cambridge University Press, 2016
3. Ole Benedictow — The Black Death, 1346–1353, Woodbridge, 2004

Reference & Online:
1. Wikipedia — Great Famine of 1315–1322 (cross-referenced against academic sources above)
2. Milton Abbas Local History Group — "The Great Famine and Pestilence 1315–1322", miltonabbashistorygroup.com

By the Late Middle Ages medieval healthcare was dominated by three main classes of medical providers. First were the university-trained physicians, fluent in Latin and immersed in learning. Then there were the untrained healers and cunning folk, who offered home remedies, herbal treatments, and specialised services such as bone-setting. Between these two worlds came the barber-surgeons, often viewed as glorified butchers. 

They handled the practical, messy, and sometimes brutal side of medicine. Not only trimming hair, but also pulling teeth, setting bones, lancing boils, and amputating limbs. Let’s travel back in time to take a look at some of the procedures that these surgeons provided.

snippet.title: Medieval Gardeners Secretly Used 10 Tricks to Grow 50% More Food
snippet.description:
Medieval gardeners didn’t have synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, or modern tools yet many of them produced surprisingly high yields from small plots of land.

In this video, we uncover 10 clever gardening techniques medieval growers used to stretch their soil, protect crops, and boost harvests long before modern agriculture took over.

You’ll Discover:

Natural soil-boosting methods that improved fertility

Companion planting tricks that reduced pests naturally

Crop rotation systems that prevented soil exhaustion

Smart spacing and layering techniques to maximize small gardens

Low-tech irrigation methods that conserved water

No chemicals. No machinery. Just practical knowledge passed down through generations.

Sometimes the old ways really were ahead of their time.

snippet.description:

For medieval women, childbirth was a perilous time, shaped as much by the limits of medicine as by the era’s beliefs and customs. Without trained physicians, modern sanitation or any dependable pain relief, labour was a trial to be endured, fraught with fear, pain and real danger. Women of every class faced the risk of death or lasting injury, even noblewomen, despite their superior care, were far from safe. 

Let’s travel back in time to take a look at just how traumatic and dangerous giving birth in the Middle ages could be, and what measures the Medievals used to help them survive the ordeal, from not giving birth in the summer, to avoiding a midwife’s big hands, and leaving cupboard doors open.
